name: Microsoft Windows
summary: Proprietary commercial operating system developed by Microsoft, founded on the hybrid Windows NT kernel and the Win32, WinUI and WSL execution subsystems.

content.introduction: Microsoft Windows is a family of commercial operating systems developed by Microsoft Corporation for personal computers, servers and professional terminals, dominant on the desktop computing market.
content.what_is_it: Initiated in its modern form in 1993 with Windows NT 3.1, Windows today rests on the unified branch of the Windows NT kernel (internal version NT 10.0 on Windows 10 and Windows 11), having definitively abandoned the old 16/32-bit MS-DOS base of the Windows 9x series.
content.kernel_architecture_and_subsystems: Windows rests on a hybrid kernel architecture (NTOSKRNL) organised in distinct modular layers: the Executive, the basic microkernel and the Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL). The Executive groups the fundamental managers of the operating system, notably the Object Manager (which manages all system primitives as secured objects), the Process and Thread Manager, the Virtual Memory Manager (VMM, orchestrating paged virtual memory and physical allocation), the I/O Manager and the Security Reference Monitor (SRM). Device drivers are organised around the Windows Driver Frameworks models (KMDF in kernel mode for critical hardware drivers and UMDF in user mode for isolated devices). In user space, applications interact with the environment subsystems through the native call library `ntdll.dll` and the Windows Win32 subsystem (orchestrated by the `csrss.exe` process), ensuring continuous binary compatibility over several decades for Win32, COM, .NET and WinUI binaries.
content.storage_security_and_hardware_anchors: The Windows security model relies on granular rights management based on access tokens, security identifiers (SID) and discretionary (DACL) and system (SACL) access control lists validated by the SRM. From Windows Vista and 7, User Account Control (UAC) separates administrative privileges from ordinary sessions. At the hardware level, contemporary versions (Windows 11) impose strict cryptographic roots of trust: UEFI Secure Boot and a TPM 2.0 (Trusted Platform Module) measuring boot integrity through PCR registers. Full storage encryption is provided by BitLocker on the NTFS file system. At the memory protection level, Windows includes Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) using the Hyper-V hypervisor to isolate a secure environment (VSM), hosting hypervisor-protected code integrity (HVCI) and Credential Guard against credential theft from RAM.
content.linux_interoperability_via_wsl: Interoperability with Linux environments is provided natively by the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). While WSL1 relied on an emulation layer translating Linux system calls into NT system calls, WSL2 relies on a Hyper-V virtual micro-machine running a real Linux kernel compiled and maintained by Microsoft. This architecture offers complete POSIX compatibility and increased system I/O performance through a VHDX (ext4) virtual file system. Integration between the two environments is close: dynamic sharing of RAM and logical processors, transparent access to Windows files through the 9P / virtio-fs protocol, a unified network bridge and graphical paravirtualisation through the d3d12 (DXCore) driver. The WSLg component adds support for Linux graphical applications and audio streams without manual configuration of an X11 server, relaying Wayland windows to the Windows desktop compositor.
content.distribution_model_and_telemetry: The Windows servicing model follows a cycle of regular cumulative updates (Patch Tuesday) and annual feature upgrades (General Availability Channel). For industrial, banking and medical production environments requiring absolute stability free of interface changes, Microsoft offers the LTSC (Long-Term Servicing Channel) channels guaranteeing 5 to 10 years of support focused exclusively on security fixes. Centralised administration relies on Active Directory (AD), Azure AD (Entra ID), Group Policy (GPO) and MDM platforms such as Intune. The system includes diagnostic telemetry services collecting usage data and hardware errors, as well as strict hardware requirements for its recent releases (excluding processors earlier than 2017/2018), imposing privacy and planned obsolescence compromises for the existing computer fleet.
content.origine_de_la_lignee_et_fin_de_windows_1: The lifecycle documentation places the current branch in a dated succession. Windows 10 was maintained until 14 October 2025, its version 22H2 being the last of that line and its editions remaining served by monthly updates until that deadline, the existing LTSC versions continuing beyond. Windows 11 begins with version 21H2, published on 4 October 2021, followed by 23H2 on 31 October 2023, 24H2 on 1 October 2024, 25H2 on 30 September 2025 and 26H1 on 10 February 2026. Each version carries a stable build number that the release health page makes it possible to follow: 22631 for 23H2, 26100 for 24H2, 26200 for 25H2 and 28000 for 26H1. The Windows 11 Enterprise lifecycle page states two scope points: version 26H2 is the last to support devices equipped with a Snapdragon 850 processor, and 26H1 is not designed as an in-place upgrade for existing devices, but for devices put on the market in early 2026.
content.canaux_de_maintenance_et_duree_de_servic: The servicing model distinguishes two types of publication. Quality updates bring security and reliability fixes, and can add features; feature updates appear once a year and serve as the basis for the maintenance timeline of the system. Three channels distribute the devices: the general availability channel, which receives feature updates as soon as they are published, the long-term servicing channel, reserved for specialised devices and receiving a new version every two to three years, and the Insider programme, which serves for testing. End-of-service dates are published per version: 26H1 is serviced until 14 March 2028 with extended support until 13 March 2029, 25H2 until 12 October 2027 and until 10 October 2028, 24H2 until 12 October 2027 in extended support, 23H2 until 10 November 2026. For LTSC editions, version 24H2 is serviced until 9 October 2029 in standard support and until 10 October 2034 for IoT Enterprise, the Enterprise LTSC 2024 edition having no extended support. The last revision published as of 13 October 2026 carries the designation 2026-10 B.
content.package_management_and_software_sources: Windows is not administered through a single package manager, but the system has included a documented command-line manager since Windows 10. WinGet is the client of the Windows Package Manager service; it is distributed in the App Installer package, itself a system component supplied and updated by the Microsoft Store on desktop editions, and by updates on Windows Server 2025. The client is supported only from Windows 10 version 1809, build 17763, and is available only after a first sign-in, the Store then registering the manager asynchronously; if the registration has not taken place, the documentation gives the command `Add-AppxPackage -RegisterByFamilyName -MainPackage Microsoft.DesktopAppInstaller_8wekyb3d8bbwe`. Features under development are obtained through a preview version, either by download or through the Canary and Dev channels of the Insider programme. Applications come from a community repository to which a publisher submits a manifest validated by the dedicated tool, and installation runs with or without elevation depending on the rights of the console.
content.installation_et_conditions_materielles: Installation and upgrade are framed by published hardware requirements. Windows 11 requires a compatible 64-bit processor at 1 GHz or more with at least two cores, 4 GB of memory, 64 GB of available disk space, a DirectX 12 compatible graphics card with a WDDM 2.0 driver, UEFI firmware capable of Secure Boot, a TPM 2.0 module, a screen of at least 9 inches at 720p and 8 bits per channel, and an Internet connection for updates. The Home edition additionally requires a connection and a Microsoft account during the initial setup. A direct upgrade from Windows 10 assumes two cumulative conditions: running version 2004 or later and having applied the security update of 14 September 2021. S mode is supported only on the Home edition, and its deactivation is irreversible; the other editions must leave it before the upgrade. The system is also supported on a virtual machine.
content.community_manifest_repository_and_instal: The default source of the Windows Package Manager is a public repository of manifest files, separate from the open-source client. The repository states which installer formats it accepts: MSIX, MSI, APPX, MSIXBundle, APPXBundle and .exe applications, plus font files in .ttf, .ttc, .otf, .otc and .fnt, for which community submissions are not yet open. Script-based installers are explicitly not supported. Contributions go through a pull request on which an automated bot determines whether a Contributor License Agreement is needed, and the repository documents the separate steps of authoring a manifest, testing it and submitting it, along with request procedures for a new package or a new version of an existing package. Private hosting of packages is documented separately from the public source, which places the default catalogue, the private catalogue and the client itself in three distinct objects.
advantages: Widest software compatibility and hardware support on the desktop market
Video game and professional application ecosystem through DirectX 12 and Win32
Integration of cross-platform development tools and of native Linux through WSL2
Robust centralised administration in enterprises through Active Directory, Group Policy and Microsoft Intune
Advanced hardware security features (BitLocker, TPM 2.0, HVCI, Windows Hello)
disadvantages: Closed proprietary software with source code under trade secret
Built-in telemetry data collection and increased incentive towards the publisher's cloud services
Strict hardware requirements imposed on recent versions (TPM 2.0, Secure Boot, recent processors)
Historically high attack surface making the system the main target of ransomware and malware
who_is_it_for: General public users and gamers looking for immediate compatibility with all game titles
Enterprises and administrations deploying workstation fleets managed under Active Directory
Developers using the Visual Studio suite, the .NET ecosystem or the WSL2 / Linux coupling
who_is_it_not_for: Users requiring digital sovereignty and full control of their system through free code
Infrastructures requiring a lightweight operating system devoid of telemetry components
Owners of old computer hardware declared unsupported by recent versions
content.verdict: Microsoft Windows is a mainstream and professional operating system published by Microsoft, combining several decades of software backwards compatibility with the NT kernel and an integrated Linux layer through WSL2.
